statement: A sentence is the largest syntactic unit and sentences occur in sequence in a text without generally being contained in one another; a clause is a construction of subject plus predicate (in central cases) and can be embedded inside a larger one.
condition: Applies when deciding whether a stretch of text is a sentence or a clause: it is a sentence only if it is one of the units occurring in succession in a text, and a clause if it has subject-predicate structure in the central cases; the same string can be a sentence in one text and merely part of a sentence in another.

correct.text: Mara left early.
correct.note: Standalone: both a sentence and a clause.

correct.text: Mara left early, but Jon stayed.

contrast.text: I heard that Mara left early.
contrast.note: 'Mara left early' is a clause here but not a sentence; it is only part of one.

review_notes: Also records that relations between sentences in a discourse are outside the book's grammar (p. 44); not made a rule.

concept: sentence has the form of a clause or clause-coordination
statement: A sentence has either the form of a clause or the form of a coordination of clauses; 'clause', not 'sentence', is the syntactic category used in constituent-structure trees.
condition: Applies when assigning a category to the top node of a constituent-structure analysis of a sentence: a sentence with one subject-predicate structure (with or without embedded clauses) is labelled clause; a sentence of coordinated clauses is labelled clause-coordination; the label 'sentence' is not used for syntactic categories.

correct.text: The dog barked.
The dog barked, and the cat ran off.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge rejects 'sentence' as a syntactic category label; Burton-Roberts's usage not checked.

review_notes: Reasons given on p. 45: (a) treating a coordination and its coordinate parts as one category fails for mixed coordinations; (b) it clashes with the everyday sense of 'sentence'. These are Cambridge's analytical arguments, not tested constraints.

statement: A coordination belongs to a different category from its coordinate parts and is named by what it coordinates: clause-coordination, NP-coordination, or a mixed form such as NP/clause-coordination.
condition: Applies to any coordinative construction: the whole is categorised as a coordination of the categories of its parts, and is not assigned the category of any single coordinate; mixed coordinations (e.g. a noun phrase joined to a clause) have a mixed label.

correct.text: You should ask [the price and whether we can pay by card].
Mara and her brother arrived.
We can meet after lunch or on Saturday. [NP/PP mixed coordination in temporal adjunct function]

review_notes: Detailed treatment is in Ch. 15; this record covers only the Ch. 2 overview. Chapter 15 §1.1 confirms coordination is a non-headed syntactic category, and a mixed NP/PP-coordination cannot be categorised as either a simple NP or a simple PP; labels reflect coordinate categories.

statement: Cambridge treats the traditional simple/complex/compound trichotomy as conflating two independent dimensions, embedding and coordination, and so uses non-compound (clausal) vs compound instead, making little further use of simple vs complex.
condition: Applies when classifying a sentence by clause structure: embedding (presence of a subordinate clause) and coordination (presence of coordinated clauses) are independent; a sentence can have both, one, or neither.

correct.text: Mara left.
I think Mara left, but Jon stayed.

statement: Canonical clauses are the basic constructions (positive, declarative, active, main, non-coordinate); non-canonical clauses differ from them along one or more of five dimensions: polarity, clause type, information packaging (e.g. passive), subordination, and coordination.
condition: Applies when describing a clause: compare it with its canonical counterpart on each of five independent dimensions: polarity (negative), clause type (interrogative, exclamative, imperative), packaging (passive, preposing, existential, it-cleft), subordination (subordinate), coordination (coordinate); a clause may be non-canonical on several dimensions at once.

correct.text: Mara read the letter.
Mara did not read the letter.
The letter was read by Mara.
Did Mara read the letter?

concept: negative and interrogative counterparts: auxiliary do
statement: When a canonical clause with no auxiliary verb is made negative or interrogative, the non-canonical form adds the semantically empty auxiliary do; interrogatives also invert subject and predicator.
condition: Applies to the specific contrasts illustrated on p. 46 (a positive declarative clause without an auxiliary versus its negative or interrogative counterpart); the full conditions on do-support are given elsewhere in the book (Chs. 3, 9, 10), not here.

correct.text: Mara did not read the letter.
Did Mara read the letter?

statement: A subordinate clause is embedded in a matrix clause; subordination can repeat, so a matrix clause may itself be embedded in a larger one.
condition: Applies when a clause is contained within another clause: the containing clause is the matrix clause for the contained subordinate clause; a subordinate clause may be marked by a subordinator (e.g. 'that') or consist of a VP with a subordinator 'to' with subject and object unexpressed.

correct.text: Mara said that Jon was ill.
correct.note: 'Jon was ill' is subordinate; the whole is its matrix clause.

correct.text: I think Mara said that Jon was ill.
correct.note: Recursive: matrix clause embedded in a larger one.

review_notes: Cambridge notes subordinate clauses can differ from main clauses far more than by a subordinator alone (p. 47).

statement: Non-canonical dimensions can combine independently where their structural requirements permit; multiple information-packaging constructions may coexist (e.g. passive plus extraposition), but certain packaging types, notably existential formation and subject extraposition, require incompatible clause structures.
condition: Applies to any clause showing more than one non-canonical feature; each feature is analysed on its own dimension, and the counterpart for one feature retains the other features.

correct.text: I can't see why the window was not closed by Jon.
It was agreed by the panel that the meeting should end. [passive plus extraposition]

contrast.text: It wasn't written by Sue.
contrast.note: Active counterpart: 'Sue didn't write it' (still negative); positive counterpart: 'It was written by Sue' (still passive).

statement: Information-packaging and other non-canonical clauses do not always have an acceptable canonical counterpart; process expressions such as preposing or passivisation are descriptive comparisons, not literal derivations of one actual clause from another.
condition: Applies to non-canonical clauses whose construction is restricted to that form: negative clauses containing negative-polarity items such as 'any longer'; interrogatives containing 'yet'; passive-only 'say + infinitive'; existentials with no non-existential counterpart; subordinate clauses with no main-clause counterpart.

correct.text: Mara can't stay any longer.
Have they replied yet?
Liam was said by the neighbours to have moved. [passive of say + infinitival, with no ordinary active counterpart of the form 'The neighbours said Liam to have moved']
There was an interruption during the session. [existential form; ordinary alternative can be pragmatically awkward]

contrast.note: Positive counterpart of a negative: ill-formed in the intended sense (cf. p. 47 [3i]).

contrast.text: *They have replied yet.
contrast.note: Declarative counterpart of an interrogative: ill-formed (cf. p. 47 [3ii]).

Chapter 16 §1: Added §1 examples where a canonical alternative is syntactically or pragmatically unacceptable and clarified that process terms describe structural differences rather than literal transformations. statement: Terms like subject-auxiliary inversion, passivisation and relativisation are convenient descriptive labels for how a non-canonical clause differs from a canonical one, and do not claim that speakers derive one clause from another.
condition: Applies when interpreting process terminology in any chapter: such terms can always be restated in static terms (for example, 'the auxiliary comes before the subject, the reverse of canonical order'); the book is an informal descriptive grammar, not a generative one.

correct.text: Is Mara still working?
correct.note: Described as inversion; statically: auxiliary precedes subject.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Burton-Roberts may use derivational terminology; not checked.

review_notes: Includes footnote 2 on p. 48.

statement: In an interrogative subordinate clause such as 'what Liz bought', the fronted element is in the prenucleus position and the rest is the nucleus; the position it is understood to fill within the nucleus is shown by a gap co-indexed with it, rather than by relabelling the fronted element as the object.
condition: Applies to clauses where an element before the subject is understood as filling a function (such as object) inside the nucleus clause, including across further embedding: the gap occupies that function in the clause of the verb it belongs to, not in the clause where the fronted element stands.

correct.text: I wonder what Mara bought.
correct.note: 'what' is prenuclear and understood as object of 'bought'.

correct.text: I can't remember what Jon said Mara bought.
I wonder which visitor Lina invited. [subordinate interrogative with subject–predicator order]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Burton-Roberts's treatment not checked.

review_notes: The tree diagrams are on pp. 48-50; trees were not examined as images for this pass. Ch. 11 §1 p. 949 identifies prenuclear interrogative phrase plus uninverted subject–predicator order as one marker of subordinate interrogative form; the corresponding main interrogative typically has inversion.

concept: no overt object after an object gap
statement: When an element in the prenucleus is understood as the direct object of the verb in the nucleus, that object position is a gap and no overt direct object may follow the verb.
condition: Applies to an interrogative clause (e.g. subordinate, introduced by an interrogative NP like 'what') whose prenuclear NP is understood as the direct object of a transitive verb in the nucleus.
violation: An overt direct object appears after the verb whose object is already realised by the prenuclear interrogative element (e.g. 'what Mara bought a watch').

correct.text: I wonder what Mara bought.
She asked what Jon had broken.

incorrect.text: *I wonder what Mara bought a watch.
incorrect.note: Overt object duplicates the object already supplied by 'what'. Source: p. 49.

incorrect.text: *She asked what Jon had broken the vase.

review_notes: Cambridge states this only for a direct object in this section. Confirm in Ch. 12 whether the generalisation extends beyond direct objects and whether any listed exceptions (e.g. resumptive-like constructions) exist.

concept: subject-auxiliary inversion analysed with a gap
statement: Subject-auxiliary inversion is analysed as a prenucleus (the auxiliary) plus a nucleus identical to the canonical clause except that the predicator position is a gap co-indexed with the fronted auxiliary, so the grammatical relations among subject, verb and complement stay the same as in the declarative.
condition: Applies to main-clause interrogatives with inverted subject and auxiliary: the fronted auxiliary is in the prenucleus, the gap takes its place as predicator in the nucleus; wh-interrogatives therefore involve one prenucleus-plus-nucleus construction inside another.

correct.text: Is Mara ill?
correct.note: 'is' fronted; its predicator position is a gap.

correct.text: What had Jon bought?
correct.note: Nucleus 'had Jon bought' functions inside the outer nucleus.

review_notes: Diagram [8] on p. 50 was read from text only. Chapter 16 §1: Explicitly distinguished auxiliary–subject inversion from subject–dependent inversion as used in the Chapter 16 information-packaging overview. Owner-approved; no independent second-pass review.

statement: The plain form of a verb occurs in four constructions: imperative, subjunctive, TO-infinitival and bare infinitival; these are clause constructions, not inflectional forms, and 'to' is a VP subordinator.
condition: Applies to clauses whose head is a plain-form verb: imperative (Take care!), subjunctive (essential that he take care), TO-infinitival (I advise you to take care) and bare infinitival (You must take care); imperative, subjunctive and infinitival are clause types, not verb forms.

correct.text: Take care!
It is vital that she take care.
I want her to take care.
You must take care.
It matters that Ada arrive early. [finite plain-form subjunctive]
It matters for Ada to arrive early. [non-finite to-infinitival]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge treats these as clause constructions rather than verb inflections; Burton-Roberts's handling not checked.

review_notes: Ch. 14 §1.1 pp. 1173–1174 distinguishes finite imperatives/mandative subjunctives from non-finite infinitivals via to, do-negation, subject case and (when present) for.

statement: Finite and non-finite are properties of clauses (and VPs), not of verb inflection: finite clauses are headed by a primary form or by a plain form in an imperative or subjunctive; non-finite clauses by a gerund-participle, past participle or infinitival plain form.
condition: Applies when classifying a clause by the form of its head verb: finite if the head is a primary form or a plain form used in the imperative or subjunctive construction; non-finite if the head is a gerund-participle, a past participle or a plain form used in the infinitival construction.

correct.text: She writes poems. [finite]
Write soon! [finite: imperative]
I want to write poems. [non-finite]
Writing poems is fun. [non-finite]
They insisted that the gate be repaired. [finite subjunctive content clause]
They asked that the gate be repaired rather than replacing it. [finite subjunctive]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Ch. 11 §1 p. 950 confirms that finite subordinate clauses include subjunctives despite use of the plain form, as well as clauses with present, preterite or irrealis forms. Non-finite clauses include infinitival, gerund-participial and past-participial constructions. Ch. 14 §1.1 p. 1173 expressly treats gerund-participles and past participles as non-finite and present/preterite/irrealis forms as finite, with the plain form occurring in both systems.

statement: Auxiliary verbs are heads, not dependents: in 'She is writing a novel', 'is' is the head and 'writing a novel' is its complement, so 'is writing' is not a constituent.
condition: Applies to the constituent structure of clauses with an auxiliary verb followed by a non-finite verb: the auxiliary is head of the clause, the non-finite clause is its complement, and the structure parallels 'She began writing a novel'.

correct.text: She is writing a novel. [is = head; writing a novel = complement]
She began writing a novel. [same structure]

statement: Adjunct covers modifiers in clause (or VP) structure together with the related supplements (e.g. 'Unhappily' in 'Unhappily, the letter arrived too late').
condition: Applies when naming a clause-level dependent that is not a core complement: a modifier in clause or VP structure, or a related supplement detached prosodically from the clause.

correct.text: She left at noon.
Unhappily, the letter arrived too late.
I spoke to her in the garden.

statement: Adjuncts and some peripheral complements are classified by semantic function, including manner, means, instrument, act-related meaning, spatial and temporal location, source, goal, path, direction, extent, duration, aspectuality, frequency, serial order, degree, purpose, reason, result, concession, condition, domain, modality, evaluation, speech act relation and connective function.
condition: When classifying a clause-level adjunct or peripheral complement, identify its semantic contribution to the situation, proposition or speech act; categories generally differ but conditionals and reasons can also have modal or speech-act interpretations.

correct.text: She left at noon. [temporal location]
They waited for an hour. [duration]
He calls every week. [frequency]
I came to help. [purpose]
If it rains, we'll stay in. [condition]
Mina repaired the lamp with a screwdriver. [instrument]
Fortunately, the team completed the task. [evaluation]
Nevertheless, the team completed the task. [connective]

concept: not even continuation requires a negative clause
statement: A clause permits a prosodically detached continuation headed by not even only when the host clause has negative clausal polarity; an otherwise positive clause cannot take that negative continuation.
condition: When a supplementary not even + complement or adjunct follows a host clause, use the negative-clause polarity tests: the host must be a negative clause, not merely a positive clause with internal subclausal negation.
violation: A positive clause (or a clause with only subclausal negation) is followed by a 'not even ...' continuation.

correct.text: He didn't read the report, not even the summary.
They didn't visit the town, not even the museum.
She never wrote, not even a postcard.
We didn't ask anyone, not even Jon.
They couldn't find the note, not even beneath the desk. [supplementary adjunct]

incorrect.text: *He read the report, not even the summary.
*They visited the town, not even the museum.
*She wrote often, not even a postcard.
*We asked everyone, not even Jon.

review_notes: One of three diagnostic tests; the book describes it as a syntactic distribution difference between negative and positive clauses. 'Never' is treated here as clausal negation by assumption; check Ch. 9 before relying on it. Chapter 9 §1.1 p. 786 identifies not even as a prosodically detached supplement and confirms the diagnostic for negative clausal polarity; the condition is restricted to the supplementary negative continuation.

statement: In polarity-matched reduced connective continuations, negative clauses typically pair with neither/nor (or negative ... either) and positive clauses with so (or positive ... too); ordinary confirmation tags reverse the polarity of the clause to which they attach.
condition: When applying clause-polarity diagnostics to anaphorically reduced connective continuations or neutral confirmation tags, use neither/nor or either for negatives and so or too for positives, and reverse the host clause's polarity in a neutral confirmation tag. Do not generalise the pattern to all kinds of interrogative tags or all uses of connective adjuncts.

exceptions.description: Same-polarity tags are available in pragmatically distinct constructions. Positive-positive tags occur, and negative-negative tags are allowed by some speakers; these do not invalidate the reversed-polarity confirmation-tag diagnostic.

correct.text: He didn't read the report, and nor did his son.
He read the report, and so did his son.
He didn't read it, did he?
He read it, didn't he?
The actors didn't rehearse, and the crew didn't either. [negative ... either]
The actors rehearsed, and the crew did too. [positive ... too]
The actors rehearsed, did they? [positive-positive tag, pragmatically distinct from confirmation]
The actors didn't rehearse, didn't they? [same-polarity tag, accepted by some speakers with a distinct pragmatic effect]
correct.note: Some speakers accept negative-negative tags; the source distinguishes their prosody and pragmatics from neutral confirmation tags.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Described as differences in distribution, not as bans on all other combinations. Chapter 9 §1.1 pp. 786–787 explicitly distinguishes the neutral reversed-polarity confirmation tag from same-polarity tags with different intonation and pragmatic effects; it also covers connective either/too in post-clause position. The 'some speakers' limitation on negative-negative tags is preserved.

statement: A clause is syntactically negative only if negation has clausal rather than merely subclausal scope; the available diagnostics include a not even supplement, negative versus positive connective continuations, neutral reversed-polarity tags, and inversion triggered by a prenuclear negative constituent.
condition: Classify the host clause's syntactic polarity using the four diagnostics as relevant: not even supplemental continuation, neither/nor versus so connective continuation, reversed-polarity confirmation tags, and obligatory inversion when negation is marked in the prenucleus. Do not infer negative polarity from inversion alone because only and connective so can trigger it as well.

correct.text: Not for the first time, she found his behaviour offensive.
We'll do it in no time, won't we?
They were rather unfriendly, weren't they?
Not for the first time, she was late, and so was he.
Not once did the committee agree. [negative clause with prenuclear negative constituent]
After lunch, the committee didn't agree. [negative clause without prenuclear negative marker]
Only occasionally did the committee agree. [inversion by only; not proof of clausal negation]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Chapter 9 §1.1 pp. 786–787 presents four diagnostics; inversion must be combined with the other tests because it is not exclusive to negative clauses. This refinement does not pre-empt §1.2's detailed treatment of subclausal negation.

statement: Negatively oriented polarity-sensitive items (including specific senses of any, anyone, ever, yet and at all) require an appropriate licensing environment: negation and certain non-affirmative clauses are common licensers, but particular scalar and non-scalar comparisons also license such items.
condition: For a negative-polarity sense of an item such as any, anyone or ever, check for an appropriate licenser: overt negative, interrogative or conditional environments, or a scalar-inequality, scalar-equality or non-scalar-inequality comparative. A plain affirmative non-scalar equality comparison does not itself license the negative-polarity reading. Free-choice any and other distinct senses are outside this restriction.
violation: A negatively oriented item occurs in an ordinary affirmative construction without a negative, interrogative, conditional, comparative or other appropriate licenser, and the intended reading is not a distinct free-choice or otherwise licensed sense.

exceptions.description: This constraint concerns the negatively oriented sense of items such as any, not their free-choice or other independently licensed readings.
Scalar inequality, scalar equality and non-scalar inequality can license negative-polarity any/ever without overt negation; plain affirmative non-scalar equality generally does not in the same sense.

correct.text: She doesn't live here any longer.
Will you be needing me any longer?
If he waits any longer, he will miss it.
They haven't replied yet.
Anyone can enter the contest. [free-choice anyone, not the negative-polarity reading]
Rafi ran faster than anyone expected. [affirmative scalar inequality licenses anyone]
Rafi ran as quickly as he had ever run. [affirmative scalar equality licenses ever]
The painting was different from anything we had seen. [affirmative non-scalar inequality licenses anything]

incorrect.text: *She lives here any longer.
*They replied yet.
*We saw anyone at the party.
*He has ever visited us.
*The painting was the same as anything we had seen. [negative-polarity reading, with no independent licenser]

statement: Positively oriented items (somewhat, some, someone, pretty in the degree sense, already, still) favour positive contexts, so 'somewhat' is not acceptable under clausal negation.
condition: Applies to clauses with 'somewhat' (or another positively oriented item) under clausal negation: the item is not acceptable inside a negative clause.
violation: A positively oriented item such as 'somewhat' occurs inside a negative clause.

exceptions.description: The special case where the negative is used to deny or contradict a prior assertion containing the item is set aside by the source.

correct.text: He was feeling somewhat sad.
The soup was somewhat salty.
They look somewhat tired.
The film was somewhat long.

incorrect.text: *He wasn't feeling somewhat sad.
*The soup wasn't somewhat salty.
*They don't look somewhat tired.
*The film wasn't somewhat long.

statement: The scope of negation is the part of the sentence the negation applies to; it is not fixed by linear order ('need not' has need inside scope, 'must not' has must outside), and some sentences are ambiguous (a because-adjunct inside or outside the scope of not).
condition: Applies when interpreting negative clauses with quantifiers, modals or adjuncts: an item is inside the scope of the negation if it is part of what is negated; scope can differ from word order.

correct.text: Not many students passed. [many inside scope of not]
Many students did not pass. [many outside scope of not]
You need not answer. [need inside scope]
You must not answer. [must outside scope]
I didn't leave because I was angry. [ambiguous]
I didn't accept the offer because it was too costly. [ambiguous relation of negation to reason]
I didn't accept the offer just because it came from my friend. [negation over just because]
Many of the guests were not present. [many scopes over the negation]
There were not many guests present. [negative scopes over many]

statement: Clause type contrasts declaratives, closed interrogatives, open interrogatives, exclamatives and imperatives, and is a category of syntactic form distinct from meaning or use (a declarative with rising intonation can ask a question).
condition: Applies when classifying clause type by form: declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative, exclamative, imperative; form categories are kept separate from meaning and use.

Is she a good player? [closed interrogative]
How good a player is she? [open interrogative]

Play well! [imperative]
You're leaving? [declarative in form; used to ask]
Would you please close the gate? [closed interrogative clause used as a directive]
Sleep peacefully. [imperative form with wish interpretation]
What on earth are you doing? [open interrogative, exclamatory in tone]

statement: Questions are classified by their set of possible answers: polar (yes/no), alternative (a choice among stated options) and variable (an answer supplies a value for a variable).
condition: Applies to the semantic classification of questions: polar = yes or no; alternative = answers are the listed alternatives; variable = answer gives a value for the open proposition.

Is this Kim's or Pat's? [alternative]
Whose is this? [variable]

statement: Speech acts such as statements, questions and orders have illocutionary force; directive is the force typically associated with imperatives, and many forces go beyond the syntactic categories (e.g. a declarative used as a promise or apology).
condition: Applies when interpreting use rather than form: force is a matter of what the utterance does; a clause type is only typically linked to a force.

correct.text: Play well! [directive]
I promise to be home by six. [declarative used as a promise]
We apologise for the delay. [declarative used as an apology]
The meeting is now adjourned. [declarative typically conveying a statement]
Passengers should remain seated. [declarative used as directive]
Would you mind moving aside? [closed interrogative used as polite directive]

statement: Illocutionary meaning is often conveyed indirectly: a closed interrogative like 'Would you like to close the window?' is syntactically a question but is likely to be used as a polite directive.

Could you pass the salt? [closed interrogative used as request]

review_notes: Ch. 10 §1 p. 854 exemplifies conventional indirect directives expressed with declaratives and closed interrogatives; no one-to-one correspondence between form and force.

statement: Subordinate clauses are first classified as finite or non-finite, and finite ones as relative, comparative or content; content clauses are the default category without the special features of relatives and comparatives.
condition: Applies when classifying a finite subordinate clause: relative (modifies an antecedent), comparative (complement of than, as, like) or content (neither); non-finite clauses are classified separately by verb form.

correct.text: The woman who called is my aunt. [relative]
It took longer than she thought. [comparative]
He said that he was tired. [content]
She asked what they wanted. [content]
The report that Alma wanted was missing. [relative: object of wanted unexpressed]
We acquired more copies than Alma wanted. [comparative: understood complement omitted]
I know that Alma wanted the report. [content: overt object]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Ch. 11 §1 p. 950 confirms relative, comparative and content as the principal finite subordinate types; content is the default, lacking the special gap properties of relative and comparative clauses. This does not convert the descriptive default into a grammatical prohibition.

concept: no noun, adjective or adverb clauses
statement: Cambridge does not use the traditional categories noun clause, adjective clause and adverb clause: classification by word-class analogy is unsatisfactory, and many traditional adverb clauses are PPs headed by a preposition with a content clause as complement.
condition: Applies when analysing 'before you mentioned it', 'if it rains', 'because they were tired': each is a PP whose head is the preposition and whose complement is a content clause.

correct.text: I left before you arrived. [PP: before + content clause]
We'll stay in if it rains. [PP: if + content clause]
They left because they were tired. [PP: because + content clause]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge rejects the traditional functional clause categories; compare with Burton-Roberts.

review_notes: Possible cross-framework conflict, see conflicts list.

statement: Clause type applies to finite content clauses as well as main clauses: subordinate declaratives, closed interrogatives, open interrogatives and exclamatives occur, but this analysis has no subordinate imperative construction; imperatives are normally restricted to main clauses.
condition: For a subordinate content clause, classify its type as declarative, closed interrogative, open interrogative or exclamative. Do not treat a to-infinitival such as to be quiet as a subordinate imperative; apparent embedding of imperative clauses is marginal and maintains main-clause-like structure.

correct.text: I believe that she is right. [declarative]
He asked whether it was open. [closed interrogative]
She asked how tall he was. [open interrogative]
She told us what a mess it was. [exclamative]
I wonder if the door is locked. [subordinate closed interrogative]
I realise what a difficult task it is. [subordinate exclamative]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Ch. 10 §1 p. 854 confirms subordinate declarative, closed-interrogative, open-interrogative and exclamative clauses; imperatives are normally main clauses, with marginal apparent embeddings retaining main-clause-like structure (footnote). Chapter 11 is identified for subordinate clause types, and Ch. 10 §9.8 for the rejection of subordinate imperatives.

statement: In the mandative construction the content clause is subjunctive, with alternants using modal should or a non-modal tensed verb.
condition: Applies to content clauses after expressions like 'it is important/essential that': the verb is a plain-form subjunctive, or 'should' + plain form, or an ordinary tensed verb.

correct.text: It is vital that he leave early. [subjunctive]
It is vital that he should leave early. [modal should]
It is vital that he leaves early. [tensed verb]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: The book lists three alternants as options; none is marked as an error.

statement: Content clauses usually function as complement, but can also be adjuncts, including a distinct interrogative kind that serves as an exhaustive conditional adjunct.
condition: Applies to the role of a content clause in a larger clause: complement (I know you are right) or adjunct (What is the matter, that you look so worried?; He won't be satisfied whatever you give him).

correct.text: I know that you are right. [complement]
She won't be happy whatever you offer her. [exhaustive conditional adjunct]
What is the matter, that you look so upset? [adjunct]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: Direct reported speech gives the words as a main clause; indirect reported speech reports the content as a subordinate content clause.
condition: Applies to reporting: a direct report quotes the speaker's words in a main clause; an indirect report uses a subordinate clause and conveys only the content.

correct.text: Ed said, 'I shall do it today.' [direct]
Ed said that he would do it today. [indirect]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: A central relative clause modifies a nominal head and is a wh relative (with who, whom, whose, which, when, etc.), a that relative (where that is a subordinator, not a pronoun) or a bare relative (no that); in each the object position is a gap co-indexed with the antecedent.
condition: Applies to relative clauses modifying a noun: wh relatives contain a relative word that is a pro-form; in a that relative, 'that' is the subordinator also found in declarative content clauses; 'that' can be omitted (bare relative).

correct.text: Here's the book which she wrote. [wh relative]
Here's the book that she wrote. [that relative]
Here's the book she wrote. [bare relative]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: Cambridge says 'that' is a subordinator, not a pro-form; traditional view differs.

review_notes: Flag for Burton-Roberts comparison. Chapter 12 §1 p. 1033 reserves the term relative clause for clausal relative constructions; detailed formal subtypes are outside this section.

statement: Integrated relative clauses function as dependents in a larger construction; supplementary relatives are prosodically detached, and the traditional restrictive/non-restrictive labels are misleading because integrated relatives are not always semantically restrictive.
condition: Applies when classifying a relative clause: integrated = syntactically and phonologically part of the sentence; supplementary = detached from the rest of the sentence.

correct.text: The man who called is here. [integrated]
We met Mara, who had just arrived. [supplementary]
Theo consulted his aunt, who was an experienced planner. [supplementary wh-relative]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Ch. 11 §1 p. 950 explicitly describes supplementary wh-relatives as subordinate in form, though supplements are not integrated syntactic dependents.

statement: In the fused relative NP construction illustrated with what, the relative element combines the function of the nominal head with that of an element in the relative clause; the resulting constituent is an NP rather than a relative clause on its own.
condition: For a fused relative expression such as what you gave me, where the expression functions as an NP, compare it with a larger NP such as the money that you gave me: classify the whole what-expression as an NP, with no separate overt antecedent.

correct.text: I've already spent what you gave me. [fused relative NP]
She took what they offered her.
I've already spent the money which you gave me. [non-fused counterpart]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Chapter 12 §1 p. 1033 clarifies that the illustrated what-fused relative is an NP, corresponding to the entire antecedent-plus-relative NP rather than just its subordinate clause. The earlier unqualified NP wording is narrowed to NP-type fused constructions; later relative types are outside the §1 pass. User approved the refinement.

statement: Relative clauses, open interrogatives, exclamatives and some others are unbounded dependency constructions: the gap may be arbitrarily deeply embedded relative to the element it is co-indexed with.
condition: Applies to wh relatives and similar constructions: the relative word is understood as filling a gap in an embedded clause, with no grammatical limit on the depth of embedding.

correct.text: Here's the book which she wrote.
Here's the book which he said she wrote.
Here's the book which I think he said she wrote.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: In a comparative clause the element corresponding to the compared measure must be left empty: no determiner or modifier expressing the measure, and no repeated gradable adjective, appears.
condition: Applies to comparative clauses as complement of than or as: the position matching the compared quantity or degree is a gap, so an overt measure phrase or a repeated adjective is not allowed.
violation: The comparative clause contains an overt measure expression (such as 'five') or repeats the gradable adjective at the position of the compared degree.

correct.text: She wrote more plays than he wrote novels.
He's as old as I am.
They have as many cats as we have dogs.
She is taller than he is.

incorrect.text: *She wrote more plays than he wrote five novels.
*He's as old as I am old.
*She read more books than he read ten magazines.
*She is as clever as he is clever.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Stated for two examples; full conditions in Ch. 13. Do not extend to all comparatives without checking.

statement: Comparative clauses are reduced subordinate clauses used as complements of prepositions such as than, as or like; comparison may be scalar or non-scalar, and scalar equality as ... as ordinarily expresses a lower bound ('at least as'), unlike non-scalar same ... as identity comparison.
condition: When a subordinate comparative clause expresses a secondary term in a comparison, analyse it as complement of than/as/(in licensed uses) like. In scalar equality, as ... as normally means at least the standard degree; do not transfer this lower-bound interpretation to non-scalar identity constructions such as same ... as.

correct.text: She wrote more plays than he wrote novels. [inequality]
He's as old as I am. [equality]
She went to the same school as I did.
Such cakes as she made were soon eaten.
As you know, we can't accept your offer.
The new plan is as good as the old plan, possibly better. [scalar lower bound]
We chose the same plan as last month. [non-scalar identity, not a degree bound]

sources.section: §1.1 Two cross-cutting distinctions: scalar vs non-scalar, equality vs inequality

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Chapter 13 §1.1 pp. 1099–1101 distinguishes scalar lower-bound equality from non-scalar identity. This refines the earlier broad use of 'at least equal' without changing the earlier comparative-clause classification.

statement: The three principal verb-based non-finite form-types are infinitival (to- or bare), gerund-participial and past-participial; these are clause-type labels distinct from the names of inflectional verb forms, while verbless clauses are a separately recognised construction.
condition: When classifying a clause with a non-finite verbal head, identify infinitival plain-form, gerund-participle or past-participle as its form-type, and for infinitivals distinguish the presence or absence of the VP subordinator to; when a clause lacks a verb, classify it separately as verbless.

correct.text: It was her plan to leave early. [TO-infinitival]
She helped them paint the fence. [bare infinitival]
Calling the police was wise. [gerund-participial]
This is the idea suggested by Mara. [past-participial]
She stood with her hands in her pockets. [verbless]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Ch. 14 §1.1 pp. 1173–1174 explicitly defines three non-finite verbal form-types and the to-/bare distinction. Verbless constructions must not be treated as a fourth verb-inflectional form.

concept: subjects of non-finite clauses; hollow clauses
statement: The subject is optional in non-finite clauses, and subjectless VPs may constitute clauses; hollow clauses additionally contain an unexpressed non-subject element, usually recoverable from the matrix clause, whereas an omitted subject is not necessarily recoverable from that matrix.
condition: When analysing an infinitival or other non-finite clause, do not require an overt subject; diagnose a hollow clause only when an understood non-subject argument such as a direct object or the complement of a preposition is missing. For subjectful to-infinitivals, for is the clause subordinator, with detailed restrictions treated in Chapter 14 §1.3.

correct.text: Mara is hard to convince. [hollow: object missing]
This idea is worth thinking about. [hollow: preposition complement missing]
For Jon to leave now would be a mistake. [overt subject with 'for']
The brochure is easy to read. [hollow infinitival missing the object of read]
We enjoyed meeting last week. [subjectless gerund-participial, not hollow merely for lacking a subject]

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: subjects of non-finite clauses; hollow clauses
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Ch. 14 §1.1 p. 1175 expressly distinguishes optional subjects from hollow clauses and states that missing non-subjects are normally recoverable from the matrix, unlike all missing subjects.

statement: A catenative complement is a non-finite clause complement licensed by verbs such as seem, intend, believe, ask and auxiliaries, forming recursive chains; it is a separate type of complement, not an object or predicative.
condition: Applies to verb + non-finite clause: the construction is recursive (a chain of verbs and non-finite complements); simple = clause follows the verb directly; complex = an NP intervenes.

correct.text: Mara seemed to enjoy it. [simple]
Jon intended to apply. [simple]
She asked me to second her motion. [complex]
He wants to try to learn to swim. [chain]
You may be right. [auxiliary: catenative]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: A raised complement belongs semantically in a lower clause than the one in which it functions syntactically: Max in 'Max seemed to like them' and Kim in 'Everyone believed Kim to be guilty' are raised, while the intervening NPs after 'intend' and 'ask' are not.
condition: Applies to catenative constructions: test by paraphrase with a subordinate clause containing the NP ('It seemed that Max liked them').

correct.text: Mara seemed to like them. [raised: subject of seem]
Everyone believed Kim to be guilty. [raised: object of believe]
Jill intended to join the army. [not raised]
She asked me to second her motion. [not raised]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: Coordination relates two or more coordinates of equal syntactic status, usually linked by a coordinator; the required likeness is mainly a matter of function rather than category, coordination can occur almost anywhere in structure, and the number of coordinates has no grammatical limit.
condition: Applies to coordination: coordinates must be syntactically alike in function (NP/PP-coordination in an adjunct position is possible); any constituent can usually be replaced by a coordination; any number of coordinates is allowed.

correct.text: She wants to go, but she can't afford it. [clause-coordination]
I've invited the manager and her husband. [NP-coordination]
She'll be arriving tomorrow or on Friday. [NP/PP-coordination]
Kim and Pat bought two houses.
Kim bought and sold two houses.
the manager, her husband, the secretary and Alice
Lina and Omar form a committee. [joint coordination: neither participant independently forms a committee]
Lina will travel this evening or on Saturday. [NP/PP mixed coordination]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: 'In general' likeness of function; exceptions in Ch. 15. Chapter 15 §1.1 describes coordinates of equal status, usually but not necessarily linked by a coordinator; replacement of the whole by one coordinate and coordinate order reversal are diagnostics that normally, not invariably, work. The p. 1275 footnote gives joint coordination as a counterexample to independent replacement; its detailed analysis is deferred to §1.3.2.

statement: Supplementation involves an anchor and a supplement: an element semantically related to the anchor but not syntactically a dependent, prosodically detached, often an interpolation or appendage; supplementary relatives are included.
condition: Applies to detached elements such as parenthetical clauses and appended noun phrases; they are linked semantically to an anchor but are not integrated into the clause structure.

correct.text: My aunt – she lives in Paris – is visiting.
I finally volunteered, a decision I quickly regretted.
Unhappily, the letter arrived late.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Chapter 8 §1 pp. 666–667 shows evaluative supplements are detached, non-restrictive, and resistant to focus.

statement: Information-packaging constructions are syntactically non-canonical ways of presenting comparable content; they characteristically preserve the truth conditions and illocutionary force of a more basic counterpart, but not invariably. The chapter's major types are preposing, postposing, subject–dependent inversion, existential, extraposition, left dislocation, right dislocation, cleft and passive.
condition: When identifying an information-packaging construction, distinguish the relevant form among the nine major types and its basic counterpart if one is available; do not require an acceptable basic counterpart or identical truth conditions when structural licensing or quantifier–negation scope differs.

correct.text: This book I gave to Mara. [preposing]
He gave to charity all the money she had left him. [postposing]
In the bag were two knives. [inversion]
There is one guard outside. [existential]
It's clear that it's a forgery. [extraposition]
It was a bee that stung me. [cleft]
I was attacked by their dog. [passive]
Those blueprints, the curator had lost them. [left dislocation]
The curator had lost them, those blueprints. [right dislocation]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Chapter 16 §1: Qualified the typical rather than exceptionless preservation of truth conditions, added dislocation types, and retained absence of a well-formed basic counterpart in certain constructions. Owner-approved; no independent second-pass review.

concept: packaging constructions: order vs function changes
statement: In Chapter 16's overview, preposing, postposing and subject–dependent inversion are reordering constructions; existential, extraposition, left/right dislocation, cleft and passive involve realignment between semantic content and syntactic functions, typically with structural complexity or added material.
condition: When comparing a more basic clause with a packaged version, identify whether the basic syntactic relationships are preserved while linear order changes (preposing, postposing, subject–dependent inversion), or whether syntactic roles/alignment are reorganised (existential, extraposition, dislocation, cleft, passive).

correct.text: There is one guard outside. [dummy there; displaced subject: one guard]
It is obvious that he lied. [dummy it; extraposed subject]
I find it odd that nobody called. [extraposed object]
In the bag were two knives. [subject-dependent inversion]
By the door stood an unfamiliar visitor. [reordering by subject–dependent inversion]
It was near the harbour that the wreckage was discovered. [cleft and passive realignment]

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: packaging constructions: order vs function changes
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Chapter 16 §1: Expanded the two-way taxonomy to include dislocation, distinguishing reordering from realignment and avoiding a claim of overt added material in every case. Owner-approved; no independent second-pass review.

statement: A cleft clause divides its basic counterpart in two: one element is foregrounded as complement of be, the other is backgrounded in a subordinate relative clause; an it-cleft has dummy it as subject, and a pseudo-cleft uses a fused relative construction.
condition: Applies to it-clefts and pseudo-clefts: foregrounded complement of 'be', backgrounded relative clause or fused relative.

correct.text: It was a bee that stung me. [it-cleft]
It was Mara who called. [it-cleft]
What stung me was a bee. [pseudo-cleft]
What I need is a rest. [pseudo-cleft]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: In a passive the active object appears as subject, the active subject appears as the complement of 'by' (the internalised complement), and the clause contains auxiliary be with a past-participial complement; clauses with the by phrase are long passives and those without it are short passives.
condition: Applies to passives: semantic roles are realigned with syntactic functions; the by phrase is optional; be + past participle.

correct.text: I was attacked by their dog. [long passive]
I was attacked. [short passive]
Their dog attacked me. [active counterpart]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

statement: Information-packaging constructions are more constrained in discourse than basic constructions; familiarity (old vs new information) and weight (length or complexity of constituents) are two key factors, and postposing generally needs a relatively heavy constituent.
condition: Applies to the use of non-canonical packaging in discourse: old information is information assumed to be shared (discourse-old or addressee-old); heavier constituents favour postposing, lighter ones favour the default position.

correct.text: He gave to charity all the money she had saved over thirty years. [heavy object: postposing natural]
He gave ten dollars to charity. [light object: default order]

contrast.text: He gave to charity ten dollars.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts material supplied for this job.

review_notes: Pragmatic tendency, not a grammatical rule. Do not use for error detection.

concept: ordinary, modal and speech act-related uses of condition and reason adjuncts
statement: Conditional adjuncts may have basic, modal, or speech act-related readings, while reason adjuncts may express an ordinary reason or a reason for the speaker's assertion.
condition: For an if-headed conditional, distinguish a condition on the situation, a qualification of the proposition, and a comment on the speech act. For a because-headed reason adjunct, distinguish a cause or reason for the situation from grounds offered for the speaker's assertion.

contrast.text: We will train outside if the weather is dry. [ordinary conditional]
If I remember correctly, the team trains on Saturday. [modal qualification]
The team trains on Saturday, if you were wondering. [speech act-related conditional]
Leah stayed home because it was icy. [reason for action]
Leah must be home, because her bicycle is outside. [reason for asserting a conclusion]

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: ordinary, modal and speech act-related uses of condition and reason adjuncts
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

review_notes: These are a limited overlap of semantic categories, not an assertion that every conditional has all readings. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

statement: Integrated temporal-location adjuncts can typically be informational focus in alternative questions, contrastive negation and clefts, whereas evaluative supplements such as fortunately resist such focus.
condition: Compare integrated temporal-location modifiers with evaluative supplements in alternative questions, contrastive negation and it-clefts, allowing that the cleft construction has a narrower range of focal elements.

exceptions.description: It-clefts permit a narrower set of focus elements than alternative questions and contrastive negation; some -ly adverbs are less readily focused in clefts.

contrast.text: The singer arrived on Thursday. [temporal adjunct]
Was it on Thursday that the singer arrived? [cleft focus]
Fortunately, the singer arrived safely. [evaluative supplement]
?Was it fortunately that the singer arrived safely? [evaluative adjunct resists focus]
Did the boat move quickly or slowly? [alternative question]
?Was it quickly that the boat moved? [cleft with -ly adverb is less natural]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

review_notes: The source distinguishes informational from scopal focus; this is not an absolute prohibition for all adjuncts. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

statement: Restrictive adjuncts affect the assertion's truth conditions; non-restrictive evaluative adjuncts do not, while a modal adjunct can be truth-relevant despite resisting focus.
condition: Compare a temporal-location modifier, evaluative supplement and epistemic modal adjunct by whether the adjunct contributes to what would make the described proposition true.

contrast.text: The parcel arrived yesterday. [restrictive temporal qualification]
Fortunately, the parcel arrived. [non-restrictive evaluation]
The parcel probably arrived. [truth-relevant modal qualification; arrival not entailed]
Surprisingly, the committee agreed. [non-restrictive evaluation]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

review_notes: Lack of focus does not entail non-restrictiveness. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

statement: Most adjunct categories can be questioned by a suitable wh-phrase, but evaluative adjuncts cannot; both reason and purpose can be questioned by why.
condition: When selecting an interrogative to target a clause adjunct, check its semantic type: temporal location can use when, reason and purpose can both use why, whereas speaker evaluation has no corresponding adjunct wh-question.

contrast.text: When did Noor arrive? — On Monday. [temporal location]
Why did Noor open the gate? — To allow the guests in. [purpose]
Why did Noor leave? — Because she felt unwell. [reason]
Fortunately, Noor reached the station. [evaluation is not a questionably targeted adjunct]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

review_notes: Most, not all, adjunct categories are question-compatible. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

concept: scope of evaluative and modal adjuncts over frequency
statement: Evaluative and epistemic modal adjuncts can take wider semantic scope than frequency adjuncts within the same clause.
condition: When an evaluative or epistemic modal adjunct co-occurs with a frequency adjunct, distinguish the reading in which the evaluation or modality applies to the whole frequency-qualified proposition.

contrast.text: Fortunately, Iris seldom misses the train. [evaluation over seldom]
Iris probably visits the library regularly. [probably over regularly]
Happily, the team usually finishes early. [evaluation over usually]

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: scope of evaluative and modal adjuncts over frequency
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

review_notes: Do not universalise the observed scope ordering; semantic scope is not reducible to linear position. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

concept: bounding effects of goal and extent dependents
statement: A terminal goal or extent can turn an unbounded activity reading into a bounded accomplishment reading, affecting how in- and for-duration expressions combine with the clause.
condition: Compare an atelic activity lacking a terminal goal with a counterpart whose goal PP or extent NP specifies an endpoint; the latter can support a bounded reading expressed with in-duration.

contrast.text: Omar jogged for fifteen minutes. [unbounded activity]
Omar jogged to the harbour in fifteen minutes. [bounded goal]
Omar walked three kilometres in forty minutes. [measured extent]
Omar jogged along the path for fifteen minutes. [nonterminal path]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

review_notes: A semantic generalization, not an exceptionless error rule for every possible for-duration reading. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

statement: Adjuncts are most often AdvPs or PPs but can also be NPs, finite or non-finite clauses, or verbless clauses, with form and semantic function distinguished.
condition: When classifying the form of an adjunct, analyse its constituent as AdvP, PP, NP, inverted conditional finite clause, infinitival, gerund-participial, past-participial or verbless clause as licensed, rather than equating its semantic function with a syntactic category.

contrast.text: Jules responded quietly. [AdvP]
Jules responded after the inspection. [PP]
Jules arrived last Wednesday. [NP]
Had Jules received the notice, she would have replied. [finite conditional]
Jules stayed late to complete the repair. [infinitival purpose]
Noticing the smoke, Jules opened the window. [gerund-participial]
The curtains drawn, Mira switched on the lamp. [past-participial adjunct]
His hands in his pockets, Milo entered the room. [verbless adjunct]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

review_notes: With non-finite and verbless clauses the precise semantic relation is often pragmatically inferred. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed. Ch. 14 §1.1 p. 1176 contrasts non-finite complements with modifiers and supplements, including purpose infinitivals and postnominal modifiers.

concept: front central and end positions of adjuncts
statement: The coarse placement distinction for clause adjuncts is front, central, and end; more than one adjunct may appear at the front or end.
condition: When describing a clause adjunct's linear position, choose front, central or end relative to the clause structure, allowing multiple front or end adjuncts; finer central-position contrasts are treated elsewhere.

contrast.text: Fortunately, there was enough time. [front]
There was fortunately enough time. [central]
There was enough time, fortunately. [end]
Yesterday beside the river, we found a lost glove. [two front adjuncts]
We camped on the hillside for three nights. [two end adjuncts]

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: front central and end positions of adjuncts
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts source/index was provided; no comparative analysis is inferred.

review_notes: The source explicitly defers detailed central placement to §20. Owner expressly approved the extraction on 2026-11-05. Independent second-pass AI review was not performed.

concept: subject–auxiliary inversion with prenuclear negative constituents
statement: When the negation of a clause is carried by a constituent in the prenucleus, subject–auxiliary inversion is obligatory in the main clause.
condition: In a main clause with a negative constituent such as not once or at no time in prenuclear position, invert the finite auxiliary and subject; insert supportive do if needed. The trigger must be the prenuclear negative constituent, not simply the presence of negation elsewhere in the clause.
violation: A main clause begins with a negative-marked prenuclear constituent but retains uninverted subject–finite auxiliary order.

correct.text: Not once did the council meet.
At no time did the visitors complain.
After the lecture, Mina didn't feel well. [negative marker on the verb, not the prenuclear adjunct]
Only occasionally did Mina attend the lectures. [inversion triggered by only, not by a negative constituent]

incorrect.text: *Not once the council met.
*At no time the visitors complained.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: subject-auxiliary inversion after fronted negative constituent
burton_roberts_mapping.note: No Burton-Roberts chapter text or concept index was provided; no comparison is inferred.

review_notes: The diagnostic is one-way: inversion also appears with connective so and prenuclear only, so inversion alone does not prove negative clause polarity. correct.text: Is the library open?
Which desk should I use?

concept: Polar questions and the polarity of answers
statement: A polar question defines a positive answer and its negative counterpart. Yes and no track the polarity of the answer in the illustrated English pattern.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A bare yes may be disfavored after a negative question. Fragments and declaratives can also express polar questions.

correct.text: Is the printer working? — No, it isn't.
Isn't the printer working? — Yes, it is.

concept: Answer sets and form of alternative questions
statement: An alternative question presents its candidate answers through or-coordination. Spoken alternatives commonly show rising pitch on an earlier coordinate and falling pitch on the last.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The coordinates can be phrases or clauses, and there can be more than two.

correct.text: Would you like soup, salad, or noodles?
Are we meeting inside or outside?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Answer sets and form of alternative questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Polar and alternative readings of or
statement: An or sequence can offer alternative answers or form a single proposition whose truth is at issue. Either paired with or forces the latter reading in the construction described here.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The first question can be ambiguous in writing. Spoken prosody and context can disambiguate.

correct.text: Are you free on Monday or Friday?
Are you free on either Monday or Friday?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Polar and alternative readings of or
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Alternative question meaning comes from coordination. The clauses involved may have the same form as clauses expressing polar questions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Whether can appear in both coordinates in an embedded alternative question.

correct.text: Did Saira call or did Leon text?
I can't tell whether the switch is broken or whether the bulb has failed.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A polar-alternative question explicitly coordinates a proposition with its negative counterpart. A polar question expresses one proposition and derives its opposite.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Ellipsis can reduce the second coordinate. In embedded questions or not may immediately follow whether.

correct.text: Is the cabinet locked or not?
Is the cabinet locked?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Licensing of alternatives in embedded and exhaustive constructions
statement: In the illustrated frames, wonder licenses polar and alternative complements, whereas doubt takes the polar pattern. The exhaustive conditional requires an alternative reading.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The restriction concerns interpretation. An or inside a polar complement does not necessarily make that complement an alternative question.

correct.text: I wonder whether the latch is open or closed.
I'll start whether the latch is open or not.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Licensing of alternatives in embedded and exhaustive constructions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Pragmatic differences between polar and polar-alternative questions
statement: The explicit negative in a polar-alternative question can emphasize choice or exhaustiveness. Ordinary polar wording can better fit a speaker already inclined toward one answer.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Insistence is a contextual effect rather than an invariant meaning of or not.

correct.text: Have you paid the invoice?
Have you paid the invoice or not?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Pragmatic differences between polar and polar-alternative questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A variable question defines an answer by asking for a value for an interrogative variable. The question can specify a limited range of values.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An explicitly limited set of values still permits a variable question.

correct.text: Who unlocked the cabinet?
Which of the two keys unlocked it?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A main open interrogative can keep a non-subject interrogative phrase in its ordinary postverbal position without inversion. This occurs in some sustained inquiries.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An in-situ question can ask for new information rather than repeat or clarify prior speech.

correct.text: And you signed the form where?
You received how many invoices, exactly?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Infinitival open interrogatives in these constructions have no overt subject. To-infinitivals occur in headings and in some independent questions, while bare infinitivals occur mainly with why.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Independent to-infinitival questions can be literary. Bare how examples are marginal. Why not plus a plain verb commonly conveys a suggestion.

correct.text: How to repair a loose hinge
Why replace the whole cabinet?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Number and coordination of question variables
statement: An open question can ask for several values at once. Coordinated interrogative phrases can share a grammatical function or express different functions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Values for coordinated phrases need not themselves be coordinated when the phrases express different functions.

correct.text: How many coats and how many blankets should we bring?
When and where will the meeting take place?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Number and coordination of question variables
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Single fronting of uncoordinated interrogative phrases
statement: In the illustrated multi-variable questions, at most one of the uncoordinated interrogative phrases is fronted.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.
violation: Two distinct uncoordinated interrogative phrases are fronted in the same finite open question.

exceptions.description: Preserve coordination, single complex interrogative phrases, in-situ interrogatives, and separate clauses.

correct.text: What did she hand to whom?
Where did they store which boxes?

incorrect.text: What to whom did she hand?
Where which boxes did they store?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Single fronting of uncoordinated interrogative phrases
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: Two distinct uncoordinated interrogative phrases are fronted in the same finite open question.
minimal_pairs: What to whom did she hand? ||| What did she hand to whom?
Where which boxes did they store? ||| Where did they store which boxes?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: In the illustrated multi-variable questions, at most one of the uncoordinated interrogative phrases is fronted.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Front one question phrase and leave the other in its ordinary position.
false_positive_guards: When and where will they meet?
Which of these boxes did they store?
She handed what to whom?
