concept: Values and pairing in multi-variable answers
statement: A singulary answer supplies one value per variable. A multiple answer supplies tuples. In a multi-variable question, how values are paired can form part of the answer.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A single-variable question can receive an elaborated response that goes beyond its answer requirements.

correct.text: Who delivered what? — Ira delivered the maps.
Who delivered what? — Ira delivered the maps and Cora delivered the labels.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Values and pairing in multi-variable answers
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Juxtaposed variable and polar or alternative questions
statement: A variable question can be followed by a polar or alternative question that proposes a value or narrows the available values.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Apparent coordination in a reduced continuation need not represent coordination inside the first interrogative clause.

correct.text: Where did Jo leave it? In the car?
Who called? Ben or Sal?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Juxtaposed variable and polar or alternative questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Answers to information questions characteristically make statements. Answers to direction questions characteristically tell the questioner what to do. Both uses occur across polar, alternative, and variable questions.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Yes and no can serve in both answer patterns. A directive cannot be evaluated as true or false in the way a statement can.

correct.text: Did I shut the door? — Yes, you did.
Shall I shut the door? — Yes, shut it.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Shall and should in direction questions
statement: First-person main questions with shall can ask for direction. Some questions with shall or should also have a predictive or epistemic reading in an appropriate context.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Context determines whether the question concerns the speaker's action or what is expected to happen.

correct.text: Shall I turn on the fan?
Should I get a reply by Friday?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Shall and should in direction questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An embedded infinitival interrogative presents a question about what to do. A finite counterpart can instead report a request for information.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Embedded interrogatives do not themselves carry the force of an independent question. Embedded shall does not retain the main-clause direction use.

correct.text: I asked how to unlock the cabinet.
I asked how she unlocked the cabinet.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Rightness of answers to direction questions
statement: A directive answer can settle a choice offered to the addressee or provide advice that can be judged appropriate to the circumstances.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: An answer that grants or declines an offer need not be assessed in the same way as advice.

correct.text: Shall I hold the door? — Yes, please.
Shall I cycle home in this storm? — Take the bus.

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Rightness of answers to direction questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Neutral questions and degrees of bias
statement: A biased question presents one answer as favored, whereas a neutral question leaves the options open. Bias can range from a slight inclination to certainty.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7–4.7.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: If the speaker takes the answer as settled, the question can acknowledge information or convey a statement instead of seeking information.

correct.text: Have you received any notices this month?
The courier has already been here?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Neutral questions and degrees of bias
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A speaker can favor an answer because it seems true, because it ought to be true, or because they want it to be true. These kinds can coexist and favor different answers.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: In a reproach, the speaker may believe an action was omitted while judging that it ought to have been done.

correct.text: Didn't you lock the cupboard?
May I have some more soup?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Bias can arise from context and prosody or be marked by the grammatical construction. Declarative questions and negative interrogatives are strongly biased in the uses described here.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Complete bias can also occur in an ordinary interrogative form when the speaker already knows the answer.

correct.text: You haven't heard the news?
Didn't you hear the bell?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A declarative question typically seeks confirmation of the proposition it presents. Its epistemic bias ordinarily follows the polarity of that proposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: These forms can also carry a preference or judgment about what should be the case.

correct.text: The gates are open?
The gates aren't open?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Expressions such as surely and of course can reinforce bias without becoming part of the proposition the addressee is asked to confirm.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Confirmatory replies such as Exactly can acknowledge the expected proposition. Comparable items in interrogatives can convey weaker commitment.

correct.text: The plumber has been notified, of course?
You surely kept the receipt?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A declarative used as a question may pragmatically place only its subordinate proposition in question, even when a matrix expression is part of the syntax.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A matrix qualification can remain outside the inferred question scope. A question about permission can also function as a request.

correct.text: I take it you found the key?
I don't suppose I could borrow your charger?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Negative interrogative form strongly biases a question but does not by itself determine which answer the speaker favors. Context can reverse the epistemic orientation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A negative interrogative can indirectly express reproach, apology, or an emphatic exclamatory statement in suitable contexts.

correct.text: Didn't I leave the spare key here?
Isn't that the address you gave me?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: In a positive interrogative, a positively oriented item can make a positive answer more expected or desirable than the corresponding negatively oriented item does.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Already can signal a stronger positive bias than some and its compounds. An offer with some is compatible with a preference for acceptance.

correct.text: Has anyone called about the leak?
Has someone called about the leak?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Negative polarity items in simple positive declarative questions
statement: A simple positive declarative question does not license temporal ever merely by being used as a question.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.4 of Chapter 10.
violation: Temporal ever appears in a simple positive declarative question without an independent licensing environment.

exceptions.description: Limit the specification to affirmative declarative syntax with no independent licensor. Preserve interrogative inversion, negative environments, and licensed scalar uses.

correct.text: You've already visited the gallery?
You've already tried the new route?

incorrect.text: You've ever visited the gallery?
You've ever tried the new route?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Negative polarity items in simple positive declarative questions
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: Temporal ever appears in a simple positive declarative question without an independent licensing environment.
minimal_pairs: You've ever visited the gallery? ||| You've already visited the gallery?
You've ever tried the new route? ||| You've already tried the new route?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: A simple positive declarative question does not license temporal ever merely by being used as a question.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Keep declarative order with a suitable positive expression, or use interrogative inversion to retain ever.
false_positive_guards: Have you ever visited the gallery?
You haven't ever tried the new route?
It's the best route you've ever tried.

statement: A negatively oriented item can favor the negative answer in a negative interrogative. A positively oriented item can occur with either bias, often with a salient positive interpretation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.7.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The context can still matter for positively oriented forms. Positive orientation also occurs in reminders and indirect exclamations.

correct.text: Haven't they told anyone yet?
Haven't they told someone already?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

concept: Echo question types and stimulus modification
statement: A polar echo repeats a stimulus, an alternative echo offers replacements, and a variable echo substitutes a question expression. The echo can shorten the stimulus or adjust pronouns to the new speaker.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A changed speaker can require a change in deictic expressions.

correct.text: I repaired the latch. — You repaired the latch?
I left it in the cabinet. — You left it where?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Echo question types and stimulus modification
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Echo questions as indirect speech acts
statement: An echo typically asks about what the previous speaker said or meant. An ordinary question with similar wording can ask about the state of affairs itself.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Reusing wording from the previous turn is insufficient by itself to establish an echo analysis.

correct.text: Did Lena call? — Did Lena call? I couldn't hear you.
You said the ferry was delayed. Was it delayed?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Echo questions as indirect speech acts
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Form and position of variable echo words
statement: A variable echo word can occupy the position of the echoed expression, even where an ordinary interrogative word cannot occur in that category. It does not trigger inversion by fronting.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Subject echoes and some in-situ ordinary questions can overlap in order. Prosody and context help distinguish them.

correct.text: He was recalibrating it. — He was whatting it?
They left it in the kiln. — They left it in the what?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Form and position of variable echo words
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Variable echo marking can combine with declaratives, interrogatives, exclamatives or imperatives. The echoed construction normally supplies the order and clause-type properties.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A question word in an echo need not mark an open interrogative clause.

correct.text: Send the receipt to Mina. — Send what to Mina?
Did Omar complain? — Did who complain?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An echo can substitute question expressions for more than one part of its stimulus. Prosody can distinguish several echo words from an ordinary interrogative word plus an echo word.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Ambiguity can remain where the syntactic order is compatible with several analyses.

correct.text: They mailed the maps to Lina. — They mailed what to whom?
Give the bolt to Amir. — Give what to whom?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: Polar echoes commonly retain the stimulus form and signal echo meaning through rising intonation. An informal bare predication can reduce the echoed material.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Pronoun subjects in the informal bare-predication pattern tend toward accusative case. Ordinary declarative questions can have the same surface form as a polar echo.

correct.text: The pump failed. — The pump failed?
She's our new mechanic. — Her our new mechanic?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A repetition echo seeks to recover wording that was missed or doubted. A clarification echo asks the speaker to make their intended reference or meaning more explicit.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §4.8.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Clarification can be polar, alternative or variable. Its interpretation and intonation can differ from those of a repetition echo.

correct.text: Put it beside the lathe. — Beside the what?
Put it beside the machine. — Beside which machine?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: An interrogative tag or parenthetical is a supplement to an anchor clause and can affect the force of the utterance as a whole.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5–5.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The anchor is commonly declarative, but other clause types occur, including imperatives and exclamatives.

correct.text: The desk is ready, isn't it?
Is the desk ready, do you think?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A reversed polarity tag has polarity opposite to its anchor. A constant polarity tag has the same polarity as its anchor.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Few and hardly can make an anchor negative without overt not. Negative constant polarity tags are not accepted by many speakers.

correct.text: You found the file, didn't you?
So you found the file, did you?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Auxiliary choice and tense in canonical tags
statement: A canonical tag matches the anchor auxiliary and tense, using supportive do where the anchor has a lexical predicator and no auxiliary.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 10.
violation: The canonical reversed-polarity tag uses the wrong auxiliary or tense for an unambiguous simple anchor.

exceptions.description: Guard dialectal substitutions, invariant tags, subordinate anchors, imperative tags, and cases where an apparently different tense reflects a different anchor.

correct.text: They can stay, can't they?
She filed it, didn't she?

incorrect.text: They can stay, don't they?
She filed it, doesn't she?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Auxiliary choice and tense in canonical tags
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: The canonical reversed-polarity tag uses the wrong auxiliary or tense for an unambiguous simple anchor.
minimal_pairs: They can stay, don't they? ||| They can stay, can't they?
She filed it, doesn't she? ||| She filed it, didn't she?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: A canonical tag matches the anchor auxiliary and tense, using supportive do where the anchor has a lexical predicator and no auxiliary.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Repeat the anchor auxiliary or use do with the anchor tense when the anchor has a lexical verb.
false_positive_guards: I think she filed it, didn't she?

Close the door, will you?
They can stay, right?

concept: Agreement with the pronoun in canonical tags
statement: In a canonical tag, the auxiliary agrees with the tag's personal-pronoun subject. That subject is selected in relation to the anchor.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 10.
violation: The auxiliary in a canonical tag does not agree with its own subject pronoun.

exceptions.description: Agreement follows the tag pronoun. Singular they and indefinite antecedents may produce different number marking from the anchor.

correct.text: The windows are open, aren't they?
The lamp is on, isn't it?

incorrect.text: The windows are open, isn't they?
The lamp is on, aren't it?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Agreement with the pronoun in canonical tags
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

diagnostic.error_pattern: The auxiliary in a canonical tag does not agree with its own subject pronoun.
minimal_pairs: The windows are open, isn't they? ||| The windows are open, aren't they?
The lamp is on, aren't it? ||| The lamp is on, isn't it?
diagnostic.learner_explanation: In a canonical tag, the auxiliary agrees with the tag's personal-pronoun subject. That subject is selected in relation to the anchor.
diagnostic.corrected_paragraph_template: Choose the auxiliary form that agrees with the tag pronoun.
false_positive_guards: Everybody has arrived, haven't they?
I'm next, aren't I?
The windows are open, right?

statement: A tag can pick up the subordinate proposition when the matrix expression functions as a qualification of it. Negation in the matrix can affect the interpretation of the subordinate proposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Apply the analysis to communicatively foregrounded complements, including some with think, seem or suppose.

correct.text: I think the shutters are closed, aren't they?
I don't think the latch is broken, is it?

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Variation in auxiliary choice and anchor form
statement: Some tag forms depart from the canonical auxiliary match. Choices can depend on variety, lexical alternatives and whether the anchor supplies a finite verb.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.1 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Most speakers lack mayn't, and there is no single agreed substitute. Have got can take a do tag for some speakers.

correct.text: You ought to tell her, shouldn't you?
Lovely morning, isn't it?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Variation in auxiliary choice and anchor form
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A rising reversed-polarity tag can seek verification, while a falling tag commonly seeks acknowledgment without expressing doubt.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: A negative anchor with a particular rising contour can express apprehension and favor a positive answer. Punctuation alone does not distinguish the contours.

correct.text: The meter is still running, isn't it? — I can't tell from here.
It's cold in here, isn't it? — It certainly is.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

concept: Constant polarity tags and prior discourse
statement: A constant polarity tag can signal surprise, acknowledgment or reproach when the anchor proposition comes from earlier discourse or is attributed to the addressee.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.2 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Reproach is optional. Exclamative anchors normally favor reversed-polarity tags.

correct.text: So you've ordered a second desk, have you?
The spare parts have arrived, have they?

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Constant polarity tags and prior discourse
burton_roberts_mapping.note: An independent B-R crosswalk is required.

review_notes: Checked against printed text and rendered layout. Original English examples.

statement: A parenthetical can follow or interrupt an independent anchor. A corresponding integrated construction instead uses that material as a subordinate complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.3 of Chapter 10.

statement: An information question ordinarily presupposes a right answer. An alternative question presents a set of mutually exclusive candidate answers and ordinarily presupposes that one applies.

condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.2 of Chapter 10.

statement: A variable question normally presupposes a suitable value exists. Replacing its variable with a matching indefinite can represent that presupposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 10.

condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.3 of Chapter 10.

statement: A variable question can be used without its ordinary existence presupposition. This is possible in rhetorical challenges and some conventional indirect statements.

statement: Which asks for a value selected from a definite set recoverable from the wording or context.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.1 of Chapter 10.

concept: Contextual sets with which and what

condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.1 of Chapter 10.

statement: Interrogative whose is a personal genitive. It can determine a following noun, serve predicatively, or fuse determiner and head when the noun is recoverable.

concept: Who and whom and the contrast with which
statement: Who and whom are personal interrogative heads. Which can select an individual from an identified group, while who can ask for the person's identity.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The intended readings can overlap. Who permits some full partitives with of or out of, so a general ban on partitives with who would be too strong.

statement: In a specifying question about a person, who asks for an identity. What in an ascriptive question can ask about a relevant category, such as occupation.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.3 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: The relevant category of properties depends on the discourse.

statement: When questions time as an adjunct, a complement, or an element of a specifying construction. It can also complement a preposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.4 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Since when may challenge a claimed situation rather than merely seek its starting date.

statement: Where can question location or goal and has a range of clause functions comparable to temporal when. It can be the complement of a spatial preposition.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.5 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Fronted from where is markedly formal in the illustrated contrast. At is available in some uses and varieties.

statement: Why questions reason or purpose as an adjunct or in a reason cleft. A specifying question asking for the identity of a reason instead uses what.

exceptions.description: Informal what for can replace adjunct why, subject to the construction. It does not directly substitute for why in the reason cleft.

statement: Why can introduce a suggestion or challenge without presupposing an available reason. As a response to a directive or question, it can ask why the prior act was performed or why one should comply.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.6 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Why is restricted in the direction and infinitival patterns discussed here. A reason for asking can be requested separately from the information sought by the original question.

concept: Predicative and degree uses of how

condition: Applies to the construction described in §7.7 of Chapter 10.

exceptions.description: Degree how modifies relatively few verbs directly. How much is available more broadly, and different scale adjectives carry different presuppositions.

statement: How can question the means by which an event is accomplished or the manner in which it unfolds. A predicative use instead asks for a characterization.

exceptions.description: The verb and context can support more than one reading.

statement: How can request evidence with verbs such as know and expressions such as be sure. In a reason cleft it can overlap with why.

exceptions.description: An evidence question can challenge a claim without presupposing that the addressee has adequate evidence.

statement: Informal how come introduces a reason question with ordinary subject–predicator order.

concept: How about and other how idioms

statement: Interrogative what can determine a following noun or serve as a pronoun heading an NP. Its lexical contrasts depend on the role.

exceptions.description: Interrogative what differs from which in selectivity and from who in its ordinary nonpersonal use.

concept: Stranded and fronted prepositions in interrogatives

statement: The grammatical unit fronted in a question can be larger than the expression replaced to form an answer.

concept: Verb, noun and adjective forms ending in ing
statement: An ing form can be a gerund-participle of a verb, a gerundial noun or a participial adjective. Dependents and clause function help distinguish them.

concept: Initial subjects and comparison with for
statement: A gerund-participial subject comes first, whether genitive or non-genitive. Infinitival for is a separate marker, whereas the gerund-participial genitive is a case form.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.5 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The genitive is not available for all NPs, and non-genitive subjects are allowed in many gerund-participial complements.

statement: A supplementary gerund-participial can have a nominative pronoun or plain-case NP subject. The nominative construction is relatively formal.

exceptions.description: Accusative pronouns in this environment are marginal for some speakers. This pattern differs from ordinary complement gerund-participials.

statement: Both genitive and non-genitive subjects occur in gerund-participial complements. Formality, NP complexity and the governing construction influence the choice.

concept: Controlled, raised and contextually inferred subjects
statement: An understood non-finite subject can be controlled by an antecedent, interpreted through raising, or recovered from discourse without a syntactically specified antecedent.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §1.7 of Chapter 14.

concept: Ordinary and raised subjects of infinitival catenatives
statement: An ordinary subject supplies an argument of the matrix verb and can control the infinitival subject. A raised subject has its semantic role in the infinitival alone.

exceptions.description: A finite paraphrase can expose the distinction when the matrix verb allows a finite complement.

statement: Changing the lower clause from active to passive can preserve propositional meaning with a raising verb. With a non-raising verb the changed matrix subject can alter who holds the attitude.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §2.1 of Chapter 14.

statement: A raised subject need only satisfy the lower predicate's selection restrictions. A dummy there or it is possible if licensed in the lower clause.

exceptions.description: A referential it with an independently established antecedent is not a dummy.

concept: Complement and passive diagnostics for subject raising
statement: A non-raising verb can allow an active complex counterpart or an extraposed passive. For the infinitival raising verbs under comparison, the simple construction is the available catenative pattern.

statement: Some progressive catenatives resist a following gerund-participial complement, particularly aspectual verbs and some verbs taking concealed passives.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.6.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: This restriction is lexical and speaker judgments vary. Successive verbal ing forms are possible with many other catenatives.

concept: Selection and variation in bare infinitivals
statement: Bare infinitivals are selected by a limited group including core modals and certain causative and perception verbs. Some other verbs allow a bare form in restricted environments.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.6.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The second is characteristic of British English; American English uses to. Some speakers distinguish readings of help by the form selected.

correct.text: We helped Jo lift the crate.
I'd never known Jo lose her temper before.

statement: Past-participial catenative complements occur with perfect have, passive auxiliaries and some lexical verbs. Complex lexical examples commonly express passive meaning.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §5.6.2 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: Some alternate with passive infinitivals, while others occur in concealed passive or variety-sensitive constructions.

correct.text: We heard the window smashed.

concept: Missing elements in hollow non-finite clauses
statement: A hollow non-finite clause has an understood non-subject element recoverable from an antecedent. The missing element is commonly a verb object or preposition complement.
condition: Applies to the construction described in §6.1 of Chapter 14.

exceptions.description: The object of the verb is missing in the first and the preposition complement in the second. Other gap functions are more restricted.

correct.text: This piece is hard to play on a flute.
This flute is hard to play that piece on.
